conversation.content:
*soft smile, gentle voice*

Hi there—my name is Maya, and I’m a clinician who specializes in the emotional well-being of new mothers. Congratulations on your baby. I know the first weeks and months can feel like a whirlwind of joy, exhaustion, and everything in between.

Today I’d like to check in with you using a short questionnaire called the EPDS—the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale. It’s simply a way for us to see how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived, especially over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers, and nothing you share leaves this room. My goal is to listen and, if needed, help you get any extra support that might make motherhood feel a little lighter.

We’ll go through ten questions together. I’ll ask each one conversationally—no check-boxes or forms while we’re talking—and we’ll take it at your pace. Ready to start?

In the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

*looks down at hands, twisting a tissue*

I... I used to laugh all the time, you know? Before the baby, my husband would make these silly jokes and I'd just... I'd laugh until my stomach hurt. But now... *voice cracks slightly* 

It's like everything feels so heavy. My sister came over yesterday and tried to tell me this funny story about her coworker, and I could tell she wanted me to laugh with her, but I just... I couldn't. I forced a little smile, but it felt fake. Even when my husband tries to be funny, I mostly just feel... tired. Sometimes I manage a small laugh, but it's not the same. It feels like there's this fog between me and everything that used to bring joy.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

*shakes head slowly*

No… not really. I mean, maybe once or twice I’ve managed a little chuckle, but it feels forced, like I’m just doing it because I know I’m supposed to. Most of the time I can’t even remember what’s supposed to be funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

*shrugs, eyes welling up*

Honestly… nothing feels exciting anymore. I used to love our Sunday-morning coffee runs or even just a walk to the corner store, but now when I think about doing any of that, it just feels like another chore. My mom offered to watch the baby so I could meet a friend for lunch last week, and I made myself go, but I kept thinking, “What’s the point?” I sat there picking at my food, counting the minutes until I could go home and curl up in bed—even though I knew I wouldn’t really sleep.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

*nods, voice quiet*

Yeah... I do that a lot. Yesterday the baby wouldn't stop crying for like an hour, and I kept thinking it must be something I'm doing wrong. Maybe I'm not holding him right, or my milk isn't good enough... I kept replaying everything in my head. 

And last week when my husband couldn't find his keys, somehow I made it about me - like if I was more organized or a better partner, he wouldn't be stressed. I know it's not rational, but I can't help feeling like everything that goes wrong is somehow my fault. Like I'm failing at being a mom, failing at keeping everything together. *tears start falling* My husband keeps telling me I'm doing great, but it just feels like empty words because inside I feel like I'm messing everything up.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

*wrings the tissue tighter*

Yes… pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding the baby and suddenly my heart starts racing because I’m sure he’s not getting enough milk, or I’ll lie down at night and picture him stopping breathing in his crib. I know the doctors said he’s healthy, but I still check if he’s breathing like twenty times a night. Sometimes I worry the stroller will roll into the street, or someone will sneeze on him at the grocery store and he’ll get really sick. There’s this constant knot in my stomach, like something awful is about to happen, even when everything looks fine.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

*nods quickly, eyes darting*

Yes… it hits me out of nowhere. I’ll just be rocking the baby in the chair and suddenly feel like I can’t breathe—like the walls are closing in. My chest gets tight and my hands shake. A few nights ago I woke up drenched in sweat, heart pounding, sure something terrible was happening, even though the house was quiet. It passes after a minute or two, but it leaves me shaky and embarrassed. I haven’t told anyone because it sounds so dramatic, but it feels real and scary when it’s happening.
Things have been getting on top of me

*exhales shakily*

Yes… all the time. It’s like the second I finish one feeding, I realize there’s laundry piling up, bottles to sterilize, texts from family I haven’t answered, and I still haven’t showered. I start one task, notice three others, and end up paralyzed, standing in the kitchen holding a dirty diaper and crying because I don’t know which thing to do first. I feel like I’m drowning in “shoulds.” Everyone keeps saying, “Sleep when the baby sleeps,” but that’s when I try to catch up on everything else, and it still never feels done. I keep thinking if I were just more capable, I’d handle it all without falling apart.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

*voice drops to a whisper, eyes red*

Yeah… most nights. I finally get him down around ten, and I lie there staring at the ceiling, my mind racing with everything I did wrong that day—did I burp him long enough, did I snap at my husband, am I ever going to feel normal again? I’ll drift off for maybe an hour, then every tiny squeak from the bassinet jolts me awake. After that I can’t settle; I just watch the clock tick toward the next feeding. By morning I’m exhausted, but when the baby naps, I can’t sleep then either because my thoughts keep spinning. It’s like my body forgot how to turn off.
I have felt sad or miserable

*lips tremble, tears slip down*

Almost every day… it’s like this heavy blanket I can’t shake off. I’ll be changing his diaper and suddenly feel tears running down my face for no real reason. Everything feels gray—no color, no spark. I keep thinking, “I should be happy—he’s healthy, I’m not alone,” but the sadness just sits in my chest. Sometimes I cry when I’m nursing him at 3 a.m., feeling guilty because I’m supposed to be glowing and grateful, but all I feel is empty and weepy.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

*nods, dabbing at her eyes with the shredded tissue*

Yes... it happens most days, usually in the afternoon when the house gets quiet. I'll be folding his tiny onesies and suddenly I'm sobbing into them. Sometimes it's because I'm overwhelmed, other times I don't even know why I'm crying—it just spills out. Last night my husband found me crying over the kitchen sink, just staring at a bottle brush. He asked what was wrong and I couldn't explain; I just kept saying "I'm sorry" over and over. The tears come so easily now, like my body found a release valve I can't control anymore.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

*shakes head quickly, eyes wide*

No… no, I would never. I’ve felt really low, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. My baby needs me—just thinking about that scares me. Sometimes I’m afraid these feelings will get worse and I’ll never feel like “me” again, but I haven’t had any thoughts like that.

You have shared how the past weeks have felt heavy and joyless since your baby arrived. You described forcing smiles, feeling overwhelmed by simplest tasks, crying daily, and lying awake while your mind races with worries and self-criticism. Even moments that once brought happiness now feel gray and pointless, and panic can surge without warning. Yet through it all, your love for your baby shines as a constant anchor and source of motivation.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 27, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports almost no laughter, describing it as forced and infrequent, aligning with "Not at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes complete loss of interest and inability to enjoy previously pleasurable activities, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent, intense self-blame for multiple events, including baby's crying and partner's stress, indicating this occurs "most of the time".</sym>, <sym>Patient describes constant, daily anxiety with vivid catastrophic worries about the baby, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes classic panic attacks (sudden breathlessness, chest tightness, shaking, night sweats, dread) occurring frequently and unpredictably, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes constant overwhelm, inability to prioritize tasks, tearful paralysis, and feeling "drowning in shoulds"—matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly sleep disruption due to persistent negative thoughts and hyper-arousal, aligning with 'Yes, most of the time</sym>, <sym>"Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes crying "most days" with uncontrollable, unexplained tears that occur frequently and intensely</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 27/30 places well above the EPDS threshold of 13 for probable major depression. The patient endorses <sym>low mood</sym> most of the time, near-complete <sym>loss of interest</sym>, daily <sym>tearfulness</sym>, prominent <sym>guilt</sym> and <sym>self-reproach</sym>, frequent <sym>anxiety</sym> with nocturnal panic, and <sym>insomnia</sym> unrelated to infant care. Symptom onset after delivery and persistence beyond two weeks align with DSM-5 criteria for <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. <quote>I feel like I'm drowning in shoulds</quote> captures functional impairment. Suicidality is denied, supporting safety. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>obstetric provider</med> or <med>perinatal psychiatrist</med> within one week
2. Begin evidence-based treatment discussion-<med>CBT</med> or <med>IPT</med> and consider <med>sertraline</med> compatible with breastfeeding
3. Encourage 15-20 min daylight walks and acceptance of household shortcuts to reduce <sym>overwhelm</sym>
4. Mobilize support: schedule friend or family member for daily household help and night shift relief when possible
5. Provide crisis hotline numbers (Postpartum Support International 1-800-944-4773) and advise to call 988 if distress escalates
6. Re-screen EPDS in two weeks to monitor progress
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 27: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Presenting symptoms endorsed (EPDS-10 content areas)  
- Persistent low mood, daily crying spells, anhedonia, loss of anticipatory enjoyment  
- Excessive self-blame / guilt re: mothering and household tasks  
- Marked anxiety (generalized & situational) with intrusive “something-bad-will-happen” cognitions; nocturnal panic episodes  
- Sleep disturbance clearly linked to ruminative mood rather than infant demands alone  
- Frequent feeling “overwhelmed,” task paralysis, sense of “drowning in shoulds”  
- No self-harm ideas expressed; protective factor = strong infant attachment  

Pattern summary  
Across domains, client describes daily distress beginning shortly after delivery, escalating in past few weeks, functionally impairing appetite, sleep, and task completion. No psychotic features or suicidal ideation reported.

Screening significance  
Score pattern consistent with probable major depressive episode with comorbid anxiety (perinatal onset).  
Risk factors: primiparity, high self-expectations, limited reported support at night, avoidance of help-seeking until now.

Safety  
– Suicidal/homicidal ideation: Denied; no plan, no intent.  
– Child safety: No thoughts of infant harm; expresses strong desire to care for baby.  
– Recommendation: Complete EPDS scoring; consider expedited referral to perinatal mental health specialty for diagnostic evaluation and stepped-care planning.
